title: Bit population census
prompt:
How many bits of a 64-bit value are set to 1? The starter reads the value in hex (`b7a5` in the stdin box). Count them with a loop.

The usual loop: use `and` to keep only the lowest bit, add it to the count, shift the value right by one, and stop when the value is zero. Each 1 bit reaches position zero exactly once. Pick the shift with care: the hidden inputs include values with the top bit set.

## what is checked

- the count of set bits is printed on its own line
- the program exits cleanly
- the count comes from masking and shifting (`and`, `lsr`)
- the same holds for other values you do not see, 0 and all 64 bits set among them
starter:
// count how many bits of a value are set
define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)

define(value_r, x19)
define(count_r, x20)
define(bit_r, x21)

        .data
fmt_in:     .string "%llx"
fmt_out:    .string "bits set = %lld\n"

        .bss
        .balign 8
value_m:    .skip 8

        .text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        ldr     x0, =fmt_in                 // read the value, typed in hex
        ldr     x1, =value_m
        bl      scanf
        ldr     x9, =value_m
        ldr     value_r, [x9]
        mov     count_r, 0

        // TODO: while value_r is not zero, mask off its lowest bit
        // with and, add that bit to count_r, and shift value_r right
        // by one.

        ldr     x0, =fmt_out
        mov     x1, count_r
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret
